title: HEMORRHAGIC DESTRUCTION OF THE BRAIN, SUBEPENDYMAL CALCIFICATION, AND CATARACTS

relationships.phenotype: HEMORRHAGIC DESTRUCTION OF THE BRAIN, SUBEPENDYMAL CALCIFICATION, AND CATARACTS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts (HDBSCC) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene (606871) on chromosome 11q25.

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts (HDBSCC) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: we identified a homozygous mutation in the tight-junction protein gene JAM3 in a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates
checks.explanation: Abstract reports only a homozygous mutation; compound heterozygous mutations are not mentioned.

checks.claim: The JAM3 gene is located on chromosome 11q25.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity mapping identified the disease locus in this family on chromosome 11q25 with a maximum multipoint LOD score of 6.15. Sequence analysis of genes in the candidate interval uncovered a mutation in the canonical splice-donor site of intron 5 of JAM3.
checks.explanation: JAM3 lies in the 11q25 candidate interval.

paragraphs.text: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is a severe autosomal recessive disorder. It begins prenatally or around birth. The main features are bleeding into and destruction of brain tissue, enlarged ventricles, calcification beneath the ependyma (the lining of the ventricles), and congenital cataracts. Affected children have severe neurologic impairment and often die in infancy.

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is a severe autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Some members of this family had a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts begins prenatally or around birth.
checks.evidence_quote: its deficiency leading to a distinctive and catastrophic neonatal presentation of cataracts and hemorrhagic destruction of the brain.
checks.explanation: The paper describes a neonatal presentation with cataracts at birth, and one sibling was stillborn with hydrocephalus. It does not explicitly say the disorder begins prenatally.

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is characterized by bleeding into and destruction of brain tissue.
checks.evidence_quote: characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is characterized by enlarged ventricles.
checks.evidence_quote: multifocal intraparenchymal hemorrhage with associated liquefaction and massive cystic degeneration resulting in large ventricles.

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is characterized by subependymal calcification.
checks.evidence_quote: characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts is characterized by congenital cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts

checks.claim: Children affected by hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts have severe neurologic impairment.
checks.evidence_quote: All the affected children in this report had bilateral cataracts and develop progressive neurological impairment, associated with seizures in some individuals.
checks.explanation: The paper describes progressive neurological impairment, and the survivors are severely retarded.

checks.claim: Children affected by hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts often die in infancy.
checks.evidence_quote: The disorder was lethal in 7 out of the 10 cases. Death occurred in the first few weeks of life.
checks.explanation: The paper reports frequent death in early infancy.

paragraphs.text: Mochida et al. (2010) described a large consanguineous family from the Middle East with several affected children. They had congenital cataracts and intracranial hemorrhage leading to destruction of brain tissue. Neuroimaging showed ventricular enlargement and subependymal calcification. The children were severely neurologically impaired, and some died early.

checks.claim: Mochida et al. (2010) described a large consanguineous family from the Middle East with several children affected by hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: in a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates. Some members of this family had a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome
checks.explanation: The UAE is in the Middle East.

checks.claim: The affected children in the consanguineous Middle Eastern family reported by Mochida et al. (2010) had congenital cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: characterized by severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts

checks.claim: The affected children in the consanguineous Middle Eastern family reported by Mochida et al. (2010) had intracranial hemorrhage leading to destruction of brain tissue.
checks.evidence_quote: However, massive intracranial hemorrhage distinguishes these patients from others.

checks.claim: Neuroimaging of the affected children in the consanguineous Middle Eastern family reported by Mochida et al. (2010) showed ventricular enlargement.
checks.explanation: Neither ventricular enlargement nor neuroimaging is mentioned in the abstract.

checks.claim: Neuroimaging of the affected children in the consanguineous Middle Eastern family reported by Mochida et al. (2010) showed subependymal calcification.
checks.evidence_quote: severe hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts
checks.explanation: Subependymal calcification is reported, but the abstract does not say it was seen on neuroimaging.

checks.claim: The affected children in the consanguineous Middle Eastern family reported by Mochida et al. (2010) were severely neurologically impaired.
checks.explanation: Neurologic impairment is not mentioned in the abstract.

checks.claim: Some of the affected children in the consanguineous Middle Eastern family reported by Mochida et al. (2010) died early.
checks.explanation: Early death is not mentioned in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) reported additional affected individuals from consanguineous families with a similar phenotype, which further defined the clinical spectrum of the disorder.

checks.claim: Akawi et al. (2013) reported additional individuals from consanguineous families with a phenotype similar to hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: Consanguinity is evident in two of the families and the clinical features of all the affected children are listed in Supp. Table S1.
checks.explanation: Only two of the three families are consanguineous. Family 2 is described as non-consanguineous.

checks.claim: The patients reported by Akawi et al. (2013) further defined the clinical spectrum of hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: Affected members from three new families underwent detailed clinical examination including imaging of the brain. Affected individuals presented with a distinctive phenotype comprising hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and congenital cataracts.
checks.explanation: The paper delineates the clinical features in the new families.

paragraphs.text: The disorder showed autosomal recessive inheritance in the consanguineous family reported by Mochida et al. (2010).

checks.claim: Hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts showed autosomal recessive inheritance in the consanguineous family reported by Mochida et al. (2010).
checks.evidence_quote: Some members of this family had a rare autosomal-recessive syndrome

paragraphs.text: Mochida et al. (2010) used homozygosity mapping in the consanguineous family to map the disorder to chromosome 11q25.

checks.claim: Mochida et al. (2010) used homozygosity mapping in a consanguineous family to map hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts to chromosome 11q25.
checks.evidence_quote: Homozygosity mapping identified the disease locus in this family on chromosome 11q25 with a maximum multipoint LOD score of 6.15.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of the consanguineous family, Mochida et al. (2010) found a homozygous mutation in the JAM3 gene, which lies in the candidate region. The mutation segregated with the disorder. JAM3 encodes junctional adhesion molecule-3 (JAM-C), a tight-junction protein expressed in vascular endothelium. The authors proposed that loss of JAM3 function disrupts the integrity of cerebral blood vessels, causing hemorrhage.

checks.claim: Mochida et al. (2010) found a homozygous JAM3 mutation in affected members of a consanguineous family with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: we identified a homozygous mutation in the tight-junction protein gene JAM3 in a large consanguineous family from the United Arab Emirates

checks.claim: The JAM3 gene lies in the 11q25 candidate region identified by Mochida et al. (2010).
checks.evidence_quote: Sequence analysis of genes in the candidate interval uncovered a mutation in the canonical splice-donor site of intron 5 of JAM3.

checks.claim: The homozygous JAM3 mutation found by Mochida et al. (2010) segregated with the disorder in the consanguineous family.
checks.explanation: The abstract does not state that the mutation segregated with the disorder; this may be in the full text.

checks.claim: JAM3 encodes junctional adhesion molecule-3 (JAM-C), a tight-junction protein.
checks.evidence_quote: the tight-junction protein gene JAM3
checks.explanation: The abstract calls JAM3 a tight-junction protein but does not give the name junctional adhesion molecule-3 or JAM-C.

checks.claim: Junctional adhesion molecule-3 (JAM-C), encoded by JAM3, is expressed in vascular endothelium.
checks.evidence_quote: JAM3 is known to be present in vascular endothelium

checks.claim: Mochida et al. (2010) proposed that loss of JAM3 function disrupts the integrity of cerebral blood vessels, causing hemorrhage.
checks.evidence_quote: Our results suggest that JAM3 is essential for maintaining the integrity of the cerebrovascular endothelium as well as for normal lens development in humans.
checks.explanation: The authors suggest JAM3 maintains cerebrovascular endothelial integrity, but the abstract does not explicitly say that losing JAM3 causes the hemorrhage.

paragraphs.text: Akawi et al. (2013) found further JAM3 mutations in additional families with the disorder and carried out cellular studies of the mutant proteins.

checks.claim: Akawi et al. (2013) found further JAM3 mutations in additional families with hemorrhagic destruction of the brain, subependymal calcification, and cataracts.
checks.evidence_quote: Sequencing the coding exons of JAM3 revealed three novel homozygous mutations: c.2T>G (p.M1R), c.346G>A (p.E116K), and c.656G>A (p.C219Y).
checks.explanation: The paper reports new JAM3 mutations in three families.

checks.claim: Akawi et al. (2013) carried out cellular studies of the mutant JAM3 proteins.
checks.evidence_quote: Cellular studies showed that the p.C219Y mutation resulted in a significant retention of the mutated protein in the endoplasmic reticulum, suggesting a trafficking defect.
checks.explanation: The paper carried out cellular localization studies of the mutant proteins.
